task.question: A block-encoding unitary represents an operator that acts on the 2^n states of an n-qubit system register, using a auxiliary qubits. (a) What is the dimension of the square matrix representing the full unitary, and why? (b) The full index is a flattened combination of a signal/ancilla register and the system register; state which register is treated as the high-order (most significant) part of the index and which as the low-order part. (c) If one instead keeps the two registers explicit as an ordered pair (signal, system) and reads off the sub-matrix for one fixed value of the signal register, how does that sub-matrix relate to the sub-matrix obtained by projecting the single flattened unitary onto the same signal branch?

cases.worked_derivation:
Let N=2^n be the system dimension and S=2^a the signal dimension. The joint computational basis is labelled by (s,i), with 0≤s<S and 0≤i<N, so it has SN=2^a 2^n=2^(n+a) labels. Therefore the full unitary has shape 2^(n+a) × 2^(n+a); the same dimension appears in the candidate record's matrix field.

The flat index is f(s,i)=sN+i. The signal label is high-order because increasing it by one moves by an entire block of N indices, whereas changing the system label moves within that block. The signal label ranges from 0 to S−1, the system label from 0 to N−1, so f(s,i) lies in [0,SN). Distinct pairs have distinct indices (quotient and remainder modulo N recover s and i); N=2^n is always positive, even n=0.

View the same matrix as V[(r,i),(c,j)]=U[f(r,i),f(c,j)]. For any fixed signal label s, the product-register submatrix is B_s[i,j]=V[(s,i),(s,j)]=U[sN+i,sN+j]. The flattened projection onto branch s is exactly that last entry expression, equivalently (⟨s|⊗I_N) U (|s⟩⊗I_N). Equality at every pair of system indices proves equality of the matrices. This works for any valid s, not just the all-zero branch used in usual clean-block constructions, and for n=0 or a=0. No extra scaling factor occurs for mere reindexing or projection; unitarity is not needed for the equality itself.

task.question: In a finite complex matrix backend, acting with an operator on a computational-basis state (a vector with a single 1 at one position and 0 elsewhere) returns the corresponding column of the operator. Using only this fact and the linearity of matrix-vector multiplication, prove that acting with an operator A on the two-term superposition a*|left> + b*|right>, where |left> and |right> are two basis states, gives a*(column left of A) + b*(column right of A), and that the amplitude read at output row k equals a*A[k,left] + b*A[k,right]. Explain why this means a block-encoding or state-preparation witness never needs to reconstruct the whole matrix-vector product: only two named columns, or two named entries, are ever required.

cases.worked_derivation:
Let e_l and e_r be computational basis vectors in ℂ^C and A∈ℂ^{R×C}. By the supplied basis fact, A e_l=A[:,l] and A e_r=A[:,r]. Since matrix–vector multiplication over ℂ is linear, A(ae_l+be_r)=aAe_l+bAe_r=aA[:,l]+bA[:,r]. For output index k, evaluation is linear, and each column's k-th coordinate is the corresponding matrix entry. Thus (A(ae_l+be_r))_k=aA[k,l]+bA[k,r].

For a two-term witness, the full output vector is determined by the two named columns: any other matrix B with B[:,l]=A[:,l] and B[:,r]=A[:,r] gives exactly the same vector. If only the single output amplitude k is requested, equality of the two named entries alone suffices. This avoids rebuilding an arbitrary full matrix–vector product proof for this sparse input. The formula remains true when l=r or either coefficient is zero; neither distinctness nor normalization is needed. It is not a generic statement that all block-encoding or state-preparation products have two-sparse inputs, nor a constant-time lookup or circuit-cost guarantee. A dense input generally needs the contributions from every nonzero basis component.

task.question: A reversible gate flips a target bit exactly when two control bits are both1. Assume each control wire is distinct from the target, but allow the two control wires to coincide. Prove the gate is its own inverse and explain what it reduces to when the controls coincide.

cases.worked_derivation: Write b for a computational-basis bit string, c₀,c₁ for controls and t for the target. If the activation predicate b(c₀)=1 and b(c₁)=1 is false, the complete string is fixed; the unchanged predicate therefore remains false. If the conjunction is true, the update changes exactly the t coordinate. Because c₀≠t and c₁≠t, both controlling values survive the update. The second application is again active and flips the t bit back. This proves the square of the action is the identity on every basis string. If c₀=c₁=c, the conjunction b(c)=1 and b(c)=1 is just b(c)=1. Since b(c) is a binary bit, this is exactly the active branch of CX, so the two actions coincide on all strings. The raw action and its involution theorem allow this coincidence even though the ReversibleGate.ccx constructor also requires different controls.

task.question: On a two-bit string(c,t), consider the update that flips c itself when c=t=1 and otherwise does nothing. Does the familiar self-inverse proof for a two-control target flip remain valid when one control is also the target? Give a concrete collision and explain the lost hypothesis.

cases.worked_derivation: Identify coordinate 0 with c and coordinate 1 with t in the question. The raw action has control0=0, control1=1 and target=0. On a=(1,1) both controls are 1, so a maps to b=(0,1). On b the first control is zero, so b is unchanged. Since a(0)=1 and b(0)=0, the two inputs are distinct. A map sending distinct inputs to the same output is not injective and cannot be a reversible basis permutation; mapping the corresponding orthogonal basis vectors to the same basis vector would violate preservation of inner products. In particular applying the map twice to a gives b≠a. The usual distinct-target proof depends on preserving both controlling bits in the active branch; here control0=target so its required inequality fails, and the active predicate actually changes from true to false. This refers to the raw total map, not to a well-formed reversible-gate object. The equiv/theorem requires both inequalities, and the constructor has still stronger constraints.
